2.text: and all four paws. Before the opening of the fair, all the tobacco was divided,

3.text: under the inspection of deputies, into piles of one or two puds, put into leather

4.text: bags, and then sealed. It had to be quite dry and of good quality. Sprinkling

5.text: with water, which adds to the weight, was forbidden. Trade with objects of

6.text: fixed value was permitted but one day. After that the less important trade began,

7.text: which was free. Thus the chief object of value offered in trade by the Rus-

8.text: sians was made, like money, quite uniform among all the traders. The kettles,

9.text: iron or copper, were also of about the same quality. The peltries of the

10.text: Chukchee, on the contrary, varied considerably in quality and value. This

11.text: unequal position of the two trading-parties led to the strange scenes described

12.text: by Wrangell.¹ For instance, trade was opened on the ice of the river near

13.text: the fortress. When the signal was given, the Chukchee quietly remained by

14.text: their sledges; while the Russians would rush ahead, dragging their tobacco

15.text: and doing their utmost to outrun each other and to secure the best peltries.

16.text: The merchants as a body were inclined to support these regulations,

17.text: because they hoped by their means to keep the price of Russians articles

18.text: of value on a certain level, sufficiently high, and purposely so fixed; or, as

19.text: it is stated in the first draught of the regulations drawn up in the year 1811,

20.text: “Nobody has a right to make exchanges under value. On the contrary, every

21.text: one must take care to raise the price as high as possible, so that the traffic

22.text: shall be more profitable for our side.”

23.text: This is plain enough. Still in the course of time some changes in the

24.text: table became necessary. They appeared in the shape of so-called “supplements,”

25.text: added to the fixed prices. Thus in the forties of the nineteenth century 10 red

26.text: foxes were worth 1 pud of tobacco, and a kettle as supplement; 20 foxes

27.text: brought 2 puds of tobacco, a kettle, and a wolverene-skin. Individual traders,

28.text: on the contrary, were all the time trying to elude the regulations, underselling

29.text: the others, buying articles of lesser value with tobacco, selling to the Chukchee

30.text: traders on credit, which was also forbidden. Some merchants had a secret

31.text: agreement with their Chukchee friends, and put into their sealed tobacco-bags

32.text: some special “supplement.” One merchant, for instance, found a way for many

33.text: years of putting into each large bag of tobacco a small flask of alcohol. His

34.text: trade was quite prosperous. All this brought on continuous trouble, mutual

35.text: complaints, denunciation, and endless chicanery. The trespassers were punished

36.text: with the utmost severity, especially those of the poorer class. Thus in the

37.text: year 1838 a trader named Bereshnov was deprived of the right of trading for

38.text: ten years because he exchanged with one Chukchee ten pounds of tobacco

39.text: for such reindeer-skins as were not included in the table. He wanted those

40.text: skins for his sister’s clothing. In bartering for foxes, he was short by three-

41.text: fourths of a fox-skin. In the year 1842 Miastukov, a poor man, underwent
